clue.text: Game bird caught in blurry photos

indicators.note: the bird is held inside the other letters
photos that are blurry have their letters out of focus, so rearrange them

parts.note: rearranged to SHOOTP
the flightless Australian bird

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's snapshots of a game bird have all come out blurred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game bird' reads as one thing, grouse or pheasant, but 'Game' is the definition and the bird sits inside the jumbled photos.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoot-'em-up is a video game built around shooting enemies.

clue.text: Japanese scoff, upsetting setters on docked vessel

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting turns the word upside down, reading it bottom to top
a docked tail is cut short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: the setters speak of themselves as US; turned up it is SU
docked of its last letter, SHI

explanation.surface: Sailors grumble about Japanese food served aboard a ship in port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoff' is British slang for food as a noun, not mockery, and 'docked' means cut short, not moored.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is Japanese food, and scoff is informal British for food.

clue.text: Veteran audibly shuffled cards

parts.note: a veteran is old

indicators.note: take the sound of the word, not its spelling

parts.note: in card games to make the cards is to shuffle them, so shuffled cards are made

explanation.surface: An old hand at the table mixes the deck noisily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shuffled' is MADE through card-table jargon, where making the pack means shuffling it; said aloud it gives MAID.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Maid is a card game, so the answer names the cards played.

clue.text: Drink alone in a flirtatious way

parts.note: a cup of tea
one at a time, on one's own

explanation.surface: Someone having a drink on their own while flirting.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a lone drinker making eyes at the room; 'alone' supplies an adverb, matching the adverbial definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To tease someone can be to flirt with them playfully, so teasingly means flirtatiously.

clue.text: Passing reminder of internet phenomenon on broken monitor

parts.note: an idea or image that spreads online

indicators.note: the letters of the word are broken apart and rearranged

parts.note: rearranged to NTOMORI

explanation.surface: A viral image pops up as a reminder on a cracked computer screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' looks like 'fleeting', but here it means dying: the answer is a reminder of death.
explanation.definitionFit: A memento mori, Latin for 'remember you must die', is an object that reminds us of our own passing.

clue.text: Fixed up mate with stock option

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read the word from bottom to top

parts.note: farmyard sense: a ram tups a ewe, mating with her; the letters then turn up the column

explanation.surface: Someone arranged for a friend to be offered a share option.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate' is the farmyard verb, TUP, what a ram does; 'up' turns it over in a down clue, and the result also means fixed or placed.
explanation.definitionFit: Put means placed or fixed in position, and a put is an option to sell stock at a set price.

clue.text: Garlic mayonnaise: superior colloid used regularly

parts.note: A1, first-rate, written with I for 1

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals, every other one

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of cOlLoId

explanation.surface: A food scientist praises mayonnaise as a first-class emulsion.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayonnaise really is a colloid, which makes the chemistry look like the definition; 'superior' is A1.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: aioli is the Provençal name for exactly this sauce, mayonnaise pounded with garlic.

clue.text: Some propose arresting revolutionary fabulist

indicators.note: only part of the words is used
the words hold the answer inside them
turned right round, read backwards

parts.note: the letters straddle the gap: the last four of propOSE plus the A of Arresting, read backwards

explanation.surface: A radical storyteller is to be taken into custody, someone suggests.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs backwards across 'propose arresting', starting in 'propose' and taking the A of 'arresting'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop is the Greek teller of fables, the fabulist of the tortoise and the hare.

clue.text: Art school led by Boris, boundlessly imaginative at first

indicators.note: the other part comes first
what comes at first in a word is its opening letter

parts.note: bORIs without its outer letters
a gam is a school of whales

indicators.note: without its bounds, the first and last letters

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: An art college run by a creative Boris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is not a college but GAM, a group of whales.
explanation.definitionFit: Origami is the Japanese art of paper folding.

clue.text: I see rising dons prone to imprecision in prestigious universities

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read from bottom to top

parts.note: as written

indicators.note: to don is to put on, so one part is put around the other

parts.note: vague, wrapped round YLE as V-YLE-AGUE
the see, or bishop's diocese, of Ely; rising it is YLE

explanation.surface: Academics at elite universities stand up to speak loosely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I see' is not a phrase of understanding: 'see' is a diocese, here Ely, an English cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ivy League is the group of eight old, prestigious universities in the north-east US.

clue.text: Piece of pretentiousness by administrative subdivision

parts.note: putting on side is giving oneself airs
a branch of an organisation

explanation.surface: A bureaucratic department produces a bit of pomposity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' is slang for a gun, not a fragment; 'side' is British for airs and graces.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece is slang for a handgun, a sidearm worn at the hip.

clue.text: Supposing irritable hosts swear

indicators.note: one word holds the other inside it

parts.note: short-tempered
on the supposition that

explanation.surface: What if a grumpy host starts cursing?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swear' reads as cursing, but it means to declare on oath.
explanation.definitionFit: Swear in its legal sense, to state something on oath, which is what a witness does in the box.

clue.text: National spirit of Turkey articulated by Istanbul's leader

indicators.note: the leader of a word is the letter that goes in front of the rest

parts.note: first letter of Istanbul

indicators.note: spoken, so take the sound

parts.note: raki is the Turkish aniseed spirit

explanation.surface: An Istanbul official speaks of Turkey's national character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National spirit' looks like patriotism, but 'National' alone is the definition, a citizen, and the spirit is the drink raki.
explanation.definitionFit: National as a noun, a citizen of some country; the answer is a citizen of Iraq, so a definition by example.

clue.text: Sign on door of Lloyd's underwriter with denture

parts.note: a Name is an individual backer of insurance at Lloyd's of London
a dental plate holds false teeth

explanation.surface: The notice on the office door of an insurer with false teeth.
explanation.walkthrough: Lloyd's of London is the insurance market; its private underwriters are called Names.
explanation.definitionFit: A nameplate is the sign on a door giving the occupant's name.

clue.text: Curse mass beer delivery

parts.note: the physics symbol for mass
a kind of beer
a speaker's delivery, the way words are spoken

explanation.surface: Someone swears at a big shipment of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' suggests a dray at the pub door, but here it is a speaker's manner of speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A malediction is a curse, a spoken wish for harm.

clue.text: Whit appointment curtailed and put back

indicators.note: its tail, the last letter, is cut off
a word put back is set in reverse, its last letter now first

parts.note: a date is an appointment; curtailed, DAT

explanation.surface: A Whitsun meeting is cut short and postponed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whit' looks like the holiday Whitsun, but it is a tiny amount, as in 'not a whit'.
explanation.definitionFit: A whit and a tad are both a very small amount.

clue.text: Restrained method of painting walls of temple

parts.note: painting with pigment bound in egg yolk

indicators.note: the outside letters, the walls around the word

parts.note: the outer letters of TemplE

explanation.surface: A discreet technique for painting a temple's walls.
explanation.walkthrough: The walls of a temple are literally painted in tempera in many churches, which makes 'walls' look physical rather than a letter instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Temperate means moderate or self-restrained.

clue.text: Handsome Wenceslas perhaps embracing ladies?

indicators.note: one part wraps its arms around the other

parts.note: Good King Wenceslas of the carol
the ladies is a women's lavatory, a loo

explanation.surface: Was the handsome Wenceslas fond of hugging women?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good King Wenceslas' is a Christmas carol; 'ladies' is the ladies' toilet, the LOO, not women at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both adjectives describe an attractive appearance.

clue.text: Public fury over introduction of stealth taxes

parts.note: open, not hidden
anger

indicators.note: a word's introduction is where it begins, its first letter

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: Voters are furious at stealth taxes being brought in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taxes' is a verb, to strain someone, not a noun; in a down clue 'over' just puts IRE on top of S.
explanation.definitionFit: To tax someone is to wear them out, and to overtire is to exhaust.

clue.text: Spooner's figurine of canine pet

indicators.note: swap the opening sounds of two words, as Dr Spooner did

parts.note: a model of a collie, with the first sounds swapped

explanation.surface: Spooner owns a china ornament of his pet dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like the dog, but it is the verb, to pamper.
explanation.definitionFit: To mollycoddle is to pet or pamper someone excessively.

clue.text: US writer from South interrupting fat cat

indicators.note: in a down clue, read from the bottom up

parts.note: pig fat

indicators.note: breaks into the middle of the other word

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe; read from the south it is EOP

explanation.surface: An American author from the South breaks in on a rich fat cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fat cat' reads as a wealthy person, but 'fat' is LARD and 'cat' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by category: cat here covers the big cats of the wild, and the spotted leopard is one of them.

clue.text: Good American English

parts.note: abbreviation for the United States
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A nod of approval for American English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good' is the noun sense, benefit, as in 'what's the good of it?', so it swaps for use.
explanation.definitionFit: 'What good is it?' and 'what use is it?' mean the same: good as benefit is use.

clue.text: Argue angrily about doctor's offence

indicators.note: the letters are thrown about in temper
goes around the other part

parts.note: rearranged to URAGE
Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree

explanation.surface: Having a furious row about a doctor's misconduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Argue angrily' looks like one idea, but ARGUE is the fodder and 'angrily' its instruction; 'offence' is taking offence, not a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: The word survives almost only in the idiom 'take umbrage', where it means resentment felt at a slight.

clue.text: Number one fan?

parts.note: reads as the top spot, first place; in fact it is slang for oneself, as in looking after number one
reads as a supporter of some star; here a devotee of oneself, and the question mark flags the twist

explanation.surface: Someone's biggest supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number one fan' means the keenest supporter, but read as a fan of number one, oneself, it is an egomaniac.
explanation.definitionFit: An egomaniac is obsessed with themselves, looking after number one.

clue.text: Despise officer losing heart after minor injury

indicators.note: the inside is lost, leaving the outer letters

parts.note: actual bodily harm, the lesser charge of assault in English law

indicators.note: the officer's letters come after the injury's, so they are placed second

parts.note: OfficeR without its heart

explanation.surface: Someone scorns a policeman who goes soft after a slight injury.
explanation.walkthrough: ABH, actual bodily harm, is the English legal charge below GBH, grievous bodily harm.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: the answer is a stronger, more formal verb for regarding something with loathing.

clue.text: Forbidden love on flying boat

indicators.note: the letters are sent flying and land in a new order

parts.note: rearranged to TABO
zero in tennis scoring, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A secret romance conducted on a seaplane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forbidden love' reads as an illicit affair, but the definition is 'Forbidden' and love is only the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: A word borrowed from Tongan for what social or religious custom prohibits, so it swaps directly for forbidden.

clue.text: Crustless toast on income support in refuge

indicators.note: remove the outside, the crusts at each end

parts.note: tOASt without its outer letters
abbreviation for the British welfare benefit

explanation.surface: Someone living on benefits eats toast with the crusts cut off in a shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: Income Support is a British means-tested benefit, abbreviated IS.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a place of refuge, like water in a desert.

clue.text: Essentially unhappy bachelor, lost and disconcerted

indicators.note: at its essence, the middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of unhAppy
Bachelor of Arts
as in shed pounds, got rid of

explanation.surface: A miserable single man, adrift and confused.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bachelor' is not an unmarried man but the degree BA.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: both describe someone embarrassed and thrown off balance.

clue.text: Taunt policeman with face of granite

parts.note: Detective Inspector

indicators.note: the front, the first letter

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A stony-faced detective mocks a suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face of granite' suggests a stern expression, but it only gives the letter G.
explanation.definitionFit: Noun sense: a pointed remark made at someone's expense, as in 'a dig at the boss'.

clue.text: Incursions and raids on Barking

indicators.note: barking mad, so the letters go crazy

parts.note: the seven letters of both words together, to be scrambled

explanation.surface: A report of raids on Barking, a district of East London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a place in East London, but here it is 'barking mad', the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the military sense: raids pushing into enemy ground, as in 'make inroads'.

clue.text: Cockney believed that female ancestor

indicators.note: a Cockney drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: HELD, as in held a view, without its H
HER without its H

explanation.surface: A Londoner trusted that woman as a forebear.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner whose accent drops H, so both 'held' and 'her' lose it.
explanation.definitionFit: A looser sense: one's elders are those born before, the older generations, which stretches to forebears.

clue.text: Criminals dread following grand old monarch and son

indicators.note: this part comes after the other

parts.note: a grand, a thousand pounds, is G
anxious fear
Elizabeth Regina
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Crooks fear an old king and his son.
